name: Caffeine (topical)

lead: Topical caffeine is included in many under-eye creams and serums intended to reduce puffiness and dark circles. It is the same xanthine alkaloid found in coffee and tea, used here at low concentrations in a cosmetic base.
The effect is cosmetic and temporary. Some small studies show reduced swelling and improved appearance, but the evidence is limited and often uses short follow-up and company-run designs.

paras: Caffeine is a vasoconstrictor that narrows small vessels, which may reduce visible blood pooling and fluid in the thin periorbital skin. It may also act as an antioxidant and may promote lipolysis and drainage in tissue, although penetration through skin is modest and effects are short-lived.

Topical use is usually well tolerated, with occasional irritation or allergy. Product guidance generally advises avoiding contact with the eyes. Absorbed amounts are small, the evidence for product claims is limited, and the effect does not address structural causes of eye bags such as fat prolapse.

lead: Topical caffeine refers to caffeine, the xanthine alkaloid found in coffee and tea, formulated at low concentrations in creams, serums and gels. It appears in many under-eye products marketed to reduce puffiness and dark circles.[1]

Proponents and product marketing describe a temporary de-puffing effect attributed to narrowing of small blood vessels and to drainage of fluid from the thin skin around the eyes. The sources reviewed contain no controlled human trial of cosmetic caffeine products for under-eye puffiness or dark circles, so these effects have not been evaluated in the published literature reviewed here.

Published research on caffeine applied to the body surface is mostly pharmaceutical: studies of caffeine delivery through skin using lipid nanoparticle carriers, and animal and small human studies of caffeine eye drops for the lens and for intraocular pressure.[2][3][4]

paras: Caffeine is included in under-eye products for puffiness and dark circles, and sometimes in cellulite and scalp products. Its use in these products is based on the idea that it constricts vessels and may promote fluid drainage; these mechanisms are proposed in marketing and are not established by trials of finished cosmetic products in the sources reviewed.

Oral caffeine acts mainly by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain, which promotes alertness; it was first isolated from coffee in 1819.[1] How these actions translate to skin is less documented. Skin penetration is a recognised challenge for caffeine, a hydrophilic molecule, and research has examined solid lipid nanoparticles as carriers to improve its permeation through skin.[2]

In rats, caffeine applied to the eye surface reached the lens and blood in measurable amounts, with blood concentrations rising over two hours.[5] Equivalent measurements for cosmetic skin products in humans were not found in the sources reviewed.

No safety trials of cosmetic caffeine creams are included in the sources reviewed. In a rat study, caffeine eye drops at the concentration tested showed no toxicity on the ocular surface or lens.[5] Caffeine in general affects sleep and arousal when consumed, with effects varying between individuals.[6][1]
No studies found on topical caffeine for under-eye puffiness or dark circles.

Related research on other uses of caffeine at the eye: a small human study of 1% caffeine eye drops in five volunteers with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension measured intraocular pressure after instillation;[4] rat studies found that caffeine eye drops protected against UV-B and galactose-induced cataract.[3][7] A trial registered on ClinicalTrials.gov examined caffeine consumption in glaucoma patients.[8] These do not address cosmetic outcomes.
